---
title: "GMM"
---

GMM twists the model's parameters until the averages the model promises
match the averages in the data. An asset-pricing model is a list of
statements about averages: a stochastic discount factor times excess
returns has mean zero, or expected excess returns line up with betas.
Those statements are moment conditions. The data give sample averages,
and GMM chooses the unknown parameters so the sample averages are as
close to the model's zeros as possible.

This is a different estimator from the cash-flow calibration in
[`calibrate_claim`](../lrr/api.qmd). Returns never enter that path.
GMM on returns is available when the moments themselves are Euler
equations or linear factor pricing errors.

## One moment, one parameter

The model $E[R^e]=\lambda$ and a sample mean of $0.08$ give
$\hat\lambda=0.08$. The moment is matched exactly.

```{python}
import geap
import numpy as np

fit = geap.gmm.linear_factor(np.array([0.08]), np.array([1.0]))
print(fit.summary())
```

## Two moments, one parameter

Two assets and one factor cannot both be zeroed. Identity-weighted GMM
is ordinary least squares of average excess returns on betas. The
leftover vector is the pricing errors, and with more assets than
parameters those errors are how the model is tested.

```{python}
mean_ret = np.array([0.08, 0.15])
beta = np.array([1.0, 1.5])
fit = geap.gmm.linear_factor(mean_ret, beta, W="identity")
print(fit.summary())
```

The fitted $\lambda$ sits between the two asset-by-asset values $0.08$
and $0.10$. Both pricing errors are nonzero.

The SDF version is the same recipe. Power utility gives
$m_t=\delta g_t^{-\gamma}$, the sample analog is the average of
$m_t R^e_t$, and GMM chooses $(\delta,\gamma)$ to make that average
small. Details are on [Examples](examples.qmd) and the formulas are on
[Mathematical detail](math.qmd).

The long-run risks estimator in [`geap.lrr.estimation`](../lrr/estimation.qmd)
uses this GMM engine with continuously updated diagonal weights and
Hansen's Lemma 4.2 $J$-test. That is Bansal, Kiku, and Yaron (2016),
not cash-flow calibration.

The source for the estimator is Hansen (1982). Cochrane (2005) is the
asset-pricing statement of the same GMM. The bibliography is on
[References](../reference/references.qmd).
